p6c1.essay:
Part Six opens by taking the camera off its tripod. For five parts Dostoevsky has kept us inside Raskolnikov's head almost minute by minute; now the narrator steps back and summarises ‘a strange period’ from somewhere ‘long after’, admitting that the dates are muddled and that Raskolnikov later had to learn what he did from other people. I find the change of distance more frightening than another fever scene would have been. The man who planned a murder to the last loop of string now wakes under bushes on Krestovsky Island without knowing how he got there.

What the fog hides is a choice he will not look at. Notice how he behaves around solitude: the emptier the road, the more he feels ‘an uneasy presence’ beside him, and so he runs back to taverns and crowds, where he is at last ‘more solitary’. Then, sitting over a song, he decides he would rather be hunted. ‘Better the struggle again!’ A fight with Porfiry or Svidrigaïlov is something to do; without an enemy he is left alone with the thing itself, and with Sonia, whose head on his shoulder at the requiem bewilders him because he can find no disgust in it.

Razumihin's visit is the comedy the book badly needs here, and it is also a small tragedy of intelligence. He arrives to swear at his friend and leaves having deduced, with great satisfaction, that Rodya is ‘a political conspirator’. Remember that under the lamp in the corridor ([[p4c3]]) he had the truth for a moment. Now he reasons his way out of it and calls his own right guess ‘crude, nasty, vile’. Decency does that. Meanwhile Raskolnikov, very quietly, makes his will: ‘I, so to speak, give them into your keeping.’

Then comes Dostoevsky's doorway trick, the real news delivered as an afterthought by a man already leaving. The painter has confessed, and Porfiry himself explained it ‘psychologically’. Watch which word alarms Raskolnikov. A guilty man should be relieved; he is dismayed, because he was in that room in [[p4c5]] and knows Porfiry cannot believe it. The chapter ends on the oddest calm in the book, a man at the door and Raskolnikov offering him a chair with a pleased expression. And keep an ear on Svidrigaïlov's remark on the stairs about fresh air. It is about to be said again by someone who cannot have heard it.

annotations.quote: he learnt a great deal about himself from what other people told him
annotations.note: A startling admission from a novel that has until now reported his every flicker of thought. The narrator is telling us that for these days Raskolnikov is not a reliable witness even to himself, and the prose loosens accordingly: summary, guesswork, ‘two or three days’.

annotations.quote: what all men need is fresh air, fresh air... more than anything!
annotations.note: Said in a stairwell, in passing, by the man Raskolnikov fears most. The whole book has been stifling since the first page of [[p1c1]], with its garret like a cupboard and its July stench, so the phrase lands as more than small talk. Hold on to it. It comes back within the hour.

annotations.quote: It seemed strange to him that there was no trace of repugnance, no trace of disgust, no tremor in her hand.
annotations.note: He checks her hand for a tremor the way he once checked his own clothes for blood. He expected to be recoiled from after [[p5c4]] and reads her tenderness as ‘self-abnegation’, which is his word, not hers. I think he cannot yet imagine being accepted, only being forgiven at great cost.

annotations.quote: the lonelier the place was, the more he seemed to be aware of an uneasy presence near him
annotations.note: Dostoevsky will not say what the presence is. Conscience, the dead, a fear of being followed, God: the sentence allows all of them and commits to none. The practical result is the paradox of the next line, that he is only truly solitary in a crowd.

annotations.quote: No, better the struggle again! Better Porfiry again... or Svidrigaïlov.... Better some challenge again... some attack.
annotations.note: This is the most honest thing he says about himself in the chapter. Being pursued gives him an opponent and a role; peace gives him only the fact of what he did. He would rather be hunted than left to decide.

annotations.quote: I didn’t tell her you love her, because she knows that herself.
annotations.note: Raskolnikov at his most gentle, and he does it in the driest possible voice. He is settling his affairs, handing his mother and sister to the one sound man he knows, and Razumihin is too happy to notice what kind of speech this is.

annotations.quote: He’s a political conspirator! He must be.
annotations.note: A wonderfully wrong deduction, and a plausible one for the 1860s, when a gloomy ex-student with secrets was far likelier to be a radical than a murderer. Razumihin builds the whole theory in a few seconds out of a sister's visit, a letter and a remark about air.

annotations.quote: What need is there for me to drink now? You have made me drunk without wine.
annotations.note: He came in resolved on a drinking bout and leaves intoxicated on one sentence about Dounia. I love that the news of the murder case, which is the centre of the novel, is to Razumihin a footnote to this.

annotations.quote: there was such a rush of hate in his weary heart that he might have killed either of those two
annotations.note: Easy to pass over, but look at how readily the thought comes. A month ago killing was a theory he had to nerve himself toward for weeks; now it presents itself as the natural answer to an annoyance. Something in him has been lowered.

annotations.quote: when the knife is at his throat at last, he feels no fear
annotations.note: The simile explains the pleased, friendly face he puts on for his visitor. Dread lives in the waiting. Dostoevsky, who once stood on a scaffold expecting to be shot, tends to write these moments of last-minute calm with unusual authority.

links.why: The ‘too menacing and unmistakable words’ in Sonia's room that have broken his concentration are at the end of this chapter.
The scene ‘in the corridor under the lamp’ that Razumihin is now so ashamed of having understood.
The interview with Porfiry that Nikolay interrupted, and the reason Raskolnikov cannot believe Porfiry has changed his mind.

p6c2.essay:
This is the third and last of the Porfiry interviews, and it turns the first two inside out. In [[p3c5]] and [[p4c5]] the examining lawyer giggled, circled, and set traps in an office with a door that might hide anything. Now he climbs the stairs to the garret himself, asks for ‘one cigarette’, and announces that ‘openness is better between us’. The question I carry through the whole chapter is whether openness is the end of the tricks or the best trick of all. My answer, for what it is worth, is that Porfiry would not see a difference, and says so: ‘perhaps you'd better never believe it altogether — I'm made that way.’

The first movement is a recitation, and it is a strange pleasure to read, because Porfiry is retelling the novel from the other side of the door. The room was searched while Raskolnikov lay ill. Razumihin's indignant talk about the case was encouraged, to stir him up. The laughter on arriving at Porfiry's flat was read ‘plain as daylight’. Scenes we lived through in a fever turn out to have had an audience. And he is honest about the weakness of it all: the evidence is ‘psychology’, and psychology ‘can be taken two ways’. He even confesses his own excitement, the ‘throbbing heart’ of the hunter. All this while Raskolnikov is drifting toward a hope so odd it frightens him, that the man has come to apologise.

Then the portrait of Nikolay, which I think is the quiet centre of the chapter. The painter is childlike, an artist of sorts, raised among sectarians, who has taken on a crime he did not commit because ‘one must suffer’. Porfiry calls him ‘an Old Believer, or rather a dissenter’, and Garnett's English hides something the Russian reader sees at once: the word for such a dissenter is raskolnik. The false confessor carries the hero's name. He is offered as a contrast, simple faith against ‘bookish dreams’, and yet the two keep leaning toward each other, and by the end Porfiry is recommending Nikolay's remedy to the man he came to accuse.

The accusation itself is done in a whisper. ‘Why, you, Rodion Romanovitch!’ I admire how little Dostoevsky makes of it: a leap from the sofa, a twitching lip, and then a denial ‘like a frightened child caught in the act’, followed by ten minutes of silence. Ten minutes is a very long time. Nothing in the earlier duels was as unnerving as that pause, because for once neither man is performing.

What follows is not an arrest but a bargain and then a sermon. Porfiry admits he cannot prove it, hints at ‘a little fact’ he will not name (I have never been sure it exists), and offers a lighter sentence for a voluntary confession. Raskolnikov's reply is the saddest line he has: ‘I don't care about lessening the sentence!’ And Porfiry, who feared exactly that, changes register entirely. ‘Don't disdain life!’ ‘Be the sun and all will see you.’ ‘Suffering, too, is a good thing.’ This is close to what Sonia said at the end of [[p5c4]], and it is remarkable to hear it from a plump official who also wants his case closed. I do not think the two motives cancel. His diagnosis is the sharpest anyone gives: a theory that broke down and proved ‘not at all original’, a man who has already stopped believing and therefore has nothing to run away with. That wounds more than the word murderer does.

Two small things I would not want missed. Porfiry, describing himself as ‘a man with nothing to hope for’ whose ‘day is over’, is about thirty-five. And his closing words are Svidrigaïlov's from the stairs in [[p6c1]]: ‘fresh air, fresh air, fresh air!’ Raskolnikov ‘positively started’, as well he might. Two men who have never met, a libertine and a lawyer, are prescribing him the same thing. Whether Porfiry's prediction about him is right is the business of the chapters that remain.

annotations.quote: The thought that Porfiry believed him to be innocent began to make him uneasy.
annotations.note: Read that twice. He ought to want nothing more, and instead the prospect alarms him. Part of him needs to have been seen, and if Porfiry really has been fooled then the one person who understood him is gone.

annotations.quote: From a hundred rabbits you can’t make a horse, a hundred suspicions don’t make a proof, as the English proverb says
annotations.note: I know of no such English proverb, and I doubt Porfiry does either. It is typical of his patter to hang a homemade saying on a foreign authority. The point is serious, though: he is conceding in advance that he has no case.

annotations.quote: There is a mistiness and a chord vibrating in the mist.
annotations.note: Porfiry as literary critic, and a good one. He mocked the article in [[p3c5]] and now admits he was moved by it, by the ‘daring of despair’ in it. He recognises a young man's sleepless prose because, he says, he once felt the same.

annotations.quote: And do you know he is an Old Believer, or rather a dissenter?
annotations.note: In Russian the last word is raskolnik, a schismatic, one who has split from the Church. Raskolnikov's surname is built on it. Garnett's ‘dissenter’ is accurate and loses the echo entirely, so it is worth knowing that the innocent man who confessed bears, in a sense, the guilty man's name.

annotations.quote: It’s not a question of suffering for someone’s benefit, but simply, ‘one must suffer.’
annotations.note: An idea foreign to the calculating arithmetic that produced the crime, where one death was to buy a hundred good deeds. Here suffering is not a price paid for anything. Porfiry presents it as a peasant oddity, and then, a few pages on, as advice.

annotations.quote: He forgot to shut the door after him, and murdered two people for a theory.
annotations.note: The whole crime in fifteen words, by someone who was not there. He has the open door of [[p1c7]], the shaking legs, the stone. It is told in the third person about an unnamed ‘he’, which lets Raskolnikov go on hoping for one more paragraph.

annotations.quote: Raskolnikov whispered like a frightened child caught in the act
annotations.note: After a month of proud theorising about extraordinary men, the denial comes out in a child's voice. Both of them whisper through this exchange, as if the truth were something that might be overheard by the room.

annotations.quote: You made up a theory and then were ashamed that it broke down and turned out to be not at all original!
annotations.note: The cruellest and most accurate sentence in the chapter. Porfiry goes for the vanity, not the guilt. What shames Raskolnikov, he suggests, is less the blood than the discovery that his great idea was commonplace.

annotations.quote: It’s as well that you only killed the old woman.
annotations.note: A few minutes earlier Porfiry said ‘murdered two people’. Now Lizaveta has dropped out again, as she so often drops out of Raskolnikov's own thinking. Whether the slip is Porfiry's or Dostoevsky's, the second victim keeps being the one nobody counts.

annotations.quote: do leave a brief but precise note, only two lines, and mention the stone
annotations.note: Delivered as an embarrassed afterthought, and chilling for its tidiness. Having preached life for two pages, Porfiry calmly allows for the other outcome and asks only that the paperwork be complete. The lawyer and the confessor are the same man to the last line.

links.why: The first interview and the article on crime, which Porfiry now admits he jeered at only ‘to lead you on’.
The second interview, all nerves and traps, which this chapter revisits and explains from Porfiry's side.
The talk with Zametov and the return to ring the bell at the empty flat, the two acts Porfiry keeps coming back to.
Sonia's counsel to accept suffering, which Porfiry repeats here from a very different chair.

p6c3.essay:
Fresh from being named a murderer to his face, Raskolnikov worries about something else entirely, and Dostoevsky underlines it: only ‘a faint vague anxiety about his immediate future’. What presses on him is which of two people to go to. Sonia is ‘an irrevocable sentence’; he must go ‘his own way or hers’. So he goes to the third person, the one who promises something ‘new’. I read this short walk as the fork of the whole final part. He is choosing between two answers to what he has done, and for now he would rather hear the one that does not ask anything of him.

The meeting is staged as an uncanny coincidence and then taken apart. He turns down a street he never uses and there is Svidrigaïlov in a tavern window. ‘Why don't you say at once it's a miracle?’ And then the deflation: I told you the address twice, it was ‘stamped mechanically on your memory’. This is the book's habit throughout. Wherever fate seems to be at work, a plain psychological explanation stands beside it, and the plain one is usually the more disturbing. A man led precisely somewhere without knowing why is the Raskolnikov of [[p1c5]] again, coming home through the Hay Market where he had no need to go.

We finally get a long look at Svidrigaïlov, and the face is ‘like a mask’, too red, too white, too blue in the eye, wonderfully young. Everything about him is slightly too much. But what he says of himself is a confession of emptiness: ‘I am nothing, no specialty.’ The list of things he might have been, ending in ‘a photographer, a journalist’, is funny and bleak together. Women are ‘an occupation’. Without it, he says lightly, he might have to shoot himself, and when Raskolnikov picks the phrase up the bragging voice stops dead. That flinch is the truest moment he has had in the novel.

Raskolnikov, I think, comes off badly, and is meant to. He lectures on vice with real disgust, and Svidrigaïlov's reply is fair: ‘And do you pretend to strength, too?’ Then the teasing name that was already in the air an hour ago, when Porfiry caught himself sounding like ‘such a Schiller’ ([[p6c2]]). Both of the older men see a romantic under the theorist. It is the murderer who is shocked here, and the libertine who is amused at being preached to by him.

annotations.quote: Sonia stood before him as an irrevocable sentence. He must go his own way or hers.
annotations.note: The alternatives are stated barely, as two roads. ‘Sentence’ is the right legal word: he fears her more than he fears Porfiry, because she does not need evidence. And ‘his own way’ is left undefined, which is why he is on his way to Svidrigaïlov to find out what it might look like.

annotations.quote: he could only decide such questions in one way
annotations.note: The one way is ‘then I shall kill him’. The narrator puts it down to exhaustion, but it is the second time in an hour that murder has offered itself to him as the simple solution. The axe has become a habit of thought.

annotations.quote: Each knew that he was seen and watched by the other.
annotations.note: A replay, as the text says, of their first meeting at the end of [[p3c6]], when one lay pretending to sleep and the other stood in the doorway waiting him out. These two are always catching each other pretending. It is the nearest thing either has to intimacy.

annotations.quote: The address has been stamped mechanically on your memory.
annotations.note: The miracle is explained and made worse. He has been walking the city as an automaton, carrying instructions he does not remember receiving. Svidrigaïlov, of all people, turns out to be the rationalist in the room.

annotations.quote: There are few places where there are so many gloomy, strong and queer influences on the soul of man as in Petersburg.
annotations.note: The novel's own thesis about its setting, handed to its least trustworthy speaker. ‘Queer’ is Garnett's 1914 word for strange. A city of people talking to themselves in the street is, incidentally, an exact description of how we first met the hero.

annotations.quote: It was a strange face, like a mask; white and red, with bright red lips
annotations.note: Health pushed until it looks painted. The features are the ones we were given when he first appeared, following Sonia home in [[p3c4]]: the flaxen hair, the blue eyes, the crimson lips. Seen close, each is a shade too much, and the face does not seem to move with what is behind it.

annotations.quote: I am nothing, no specialty, and sometimes I am positively bored.
annotations.note: Set this beside Raskolnikov's ambition to be somebody extraordinary. Svidrigaïlov has stepped over every line there is and found on the far side not greatness but boredom. I take this to be what the ‘new’ thing Raskolnikov hoped to learn from him actually amounts to.

annotations.quote: If I hadn’t this, I might have to shoot myself.
annotations.note: Tossed off as a manner of speaking, the kind of thing a man about town says. Watch what happens to his face in the next exchange when Raskolnikov takes it literally.

annotations.quote: You preach to me about vice and æsthetics! You--a Schiller, you--an idealist!
annotations.note: Schiller stands for high-minded, beautiful-souled idealism, and in Dostoevsky it is usually said with a smile. The joke has an edge: this particular idealist has taken an axe to two women. Porfiry used the same name of himself in [[p6c2]], so the word is in the air.

links.why: Their first long conversation, with the apparitions of Marfa Petrovna and his insistence that he and Raskolnikov are alike.
Where Svidrigaïlov let Raskolnikov know what he had overheard, the ‘hidden power’ that drives this visit.
Porfiry, too, reached for Schiller an hour earlier and gave his own reading of the young man's character; the two diagnoses are worth setting side by side.
The last page, where a stranger stands in the doorway while Raskolnikov pretends to be asleep, is the scene Svidrigaïlov throws back at him here.

p6c4.essay:
Nearly the whole chapter is one man talking, and the work for the reader is deciding how much of it to believe. Svidrigaïlov tells again the story we first had in the mother's letter in [[p1c3]], the governess, the wife, the scandal, but from the side of the pursuer, and he tells it well. That is the difficulty. He is observant, funny about Marfa Petrovna's six-clause marriage contract, and candid about his own ‘swinishness’. I catch myself enjoying him and then remember what he is describing.

The most surprising thing is how accurately he sees Dounia. She would have ‘smiled when they branded her bosom with hot pincers’; she is ‘thirsting to face some torture for someone’. Put that next to what Porfiry said of her brother an hour earlier in [[p6c2]], that he is one of those who would smile at their torturer. Two men who have never spoken draw the same picture of the two siblings. And Svidrigaïlov's use of it is the sinister part: he understood that her wish to save a lost soul was the door, and he walked through it. His little lecture on flattery is a seducer's manual delivered to the brother of the woman it was used on.

Then the tone curdles. The betrothed who is not yet sixteen, taken on his knee, compared to the Sistine Madonna; the thirteen-year-old at the dance hall and her grateful mother. He says outright that he tells these things ‘on purpose, for the pleasure of hearing your outcries’, so we are being baited along with Raskolnikov. Notice too what he will not discuss, the child and the footman from Luzhin's charges in [[p4c2]]: ‘vulgar tales’. A man this talkative chooses his silences.

Under the talk there is a clock. ‘Only ten minutes left.’ He keeps checking his watch, throws the champagne out of the window when he feels he has said too much, wets a towel for his head. Something is to happen this evening and the anecdotes are filling the time before it. Raskolnikov senses that, and for once his suspicion is doing useful work.

And the parting shot is deserved. ‘You are a thorough cynic yourself.’ Raskolnikov has already admitted, ‘I can see I am ridiculous myself.’ The outrage is real, and so is the question of who is entitled to it.

annotations.quote: she always kept a clove or something in her mouth
annotations.note: One detail and the dead woman is alive, sweetening her breath for a husband who is cataloguing her faults. Svidrigaïlov's eye for this sort of thing is what makes him good company on the page and bad company in a house.

annotations.quote: would have smiled when they branded her bosom with hot pincers
annotations.note: An extravagant compliment, and a predator's assessment. Compare Porfiry on her brother in [[p6c2]], smiling at the torturer who cuts out his entrails. The family likeness is being pointed out by two different outsiders within the same afternoon.

annotations.quote: he’s said to be a sensible fellow; his surname suggests it, indeed
annotations.note: A pun the translation cannot carry. Razumihin comes from razum, reason or good sense. Dostoevsky names people pointedly, and here he has a character notice it aloud.

annotations.quote: Nothing in the world is harder than speaking the truth and nothing easier than flattery.
annotations.note: A true remark from a man explaining how he lies. His theory is that truth must be perfect to be believed while flattery works even when every note is false. Porfiry, accused of flattery in [[p6c2]], cheerfully admitted the possibility; the two chapters are in conversation.

annotations.quote: which would really have been just the same thing as I was proposing
annotations.note: His thirty thousand roubles for an elopement, and Luzhin's respectable offer of marriage: the same purchase, he says, and presses the point with ‘Wouldn't it?’ Raskolnikov cannot easily disagree. He made the same comparison himself, in a rage, in [[p1c4]].

annotations.quote: There’s always a little corner which remains a secret to the world and is only known to those two.
annotations.note: Insinuation dressed as worldly wisdom. He concedes that Dounia does not love him and in the same breath plants the idea that her brother cannot really know. It is aimed precisely, and it draws blood.

annotations.quote: Her face is like Raphael’s Madonna.
annotations.note: The Sistine Madonna, in Dresden, was a painting Dostoevsky himself revered. To put it in this mouth, about a child being bargained off by her parents, is a deliberate desecration. Svidrigaïlov has taste, and the taste makes it worse.

annotations.quote: Everyone thinks of himself, and he lives most gaily who knows best how to deceive himself.
annotations.note: His whole philosophy in a sentence, followed by a laugh. What is odd is that he does not seem to be one of the gay ones. He described himself a page back as a gloomy man who sits in a corner for three days without speaking.

annotations.quote: waste themselves in impossible dreams and visions and are crippled by theories
annotations.note: Slipped into a tirade about Petersburg, and aimed at the listener. Porfiry spoke of ‘a heart unhinged by theories’ in the previous hour. Everyone who looks at Raskolnikov arrives at the same word.

annotations.quote: if you come to that, you are a thorough cynic yourself
annotations.note: Said ‘with some surprise’, as if he had not expected the young man to see through the performance so quickly. He means it as kinship. It is the last thing Raskolnikov wants to be told, and he has no ready answer.

links.why: The mother's letter gave this same episode with Dounia and Marfa Petrovna from the family's side; read against it, his version shows what he adds and what he leaves out.
Luzhin's accusations about the child and the footman, which Svidrigaïlov twice refuses to talk about here.
Raskolnikov's own furious verdict on the Luzhin match, which Svidrigaïlov now echoes for his own purposes.
Porfiry's image of Raskolnikov smiling under torture matches the martyr Svidrigaïlov sees in Dounia.
